newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB says study supports single-desk barley sales.
newsitem.headline: CWB says study supports single-desk barley sales.

text.p: The Canadian Wheat Board said a study by four academic specialists supports the benefits of keeping CWB's single-desk monopoly sales system in barley.

"The results indicate that having only one seller of Canadian barley is worth an additional C$72 million per year compared to what would be attainable if there were many sellers of Canadian barley," the Board said in a statement.

The study, funded by the Board, comes as 80,000 Canadian barley producers are voting in a government-mandated plebiscite on whether the Board's monopoly over barley exports and domestic malting barley sales should be retained.

Debate over the power of the CWB as sole seller of Western Canadian grains has been fierce in recent years, led by Alberta farmers and officials who have demanded the government offer farmers the option of at least some private sales.
Critics claim that producer earnings from the Board's pool system of sales have not provided maximum benefits at times of high world grain prices, as in the last two years.

A federal advisory panel last year recommended that Canada retain CWB's monopoly over malting barley but create an open market in feed barley. The latter was rejected by Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale, who ordered the producer plebiscite.
About 80,000 ballots were sent to farmers January 23. They are due back by February 28 with results expected late March.

CWB is the sole marketer of Prairie six-row and two-row malting barley to the domestic and export markets and also holds a monopoly on feed barley exports. In malting barley, the CWB accounts for 40 percent of world exports.
In overall barley exports, Canada, Australia and the European Union account for up to 80 percent of the market.
CWB said the study estimated that single-desking earned six-row barley growers an average extra $42 per tonne in the 1985-1995 period and two-row growers an extra $34 per tonne.
Single-desking of feed barley, which competes with corn, earned farmers an extra $3.50 per tonne per year, it said.

CWB said the study also rejected claims that single desk sales distorted domestic and world feed barley prices due to lack of arbitrage with the pool returns, Western Canadian feed barley prices and international feed barley prices.

"These losses are small compared to the price premiums earned by the CWB," the study said. "Even so, they could have been significantly reduced by providing the CWB with added flexibility, including cash trading," it said.
The study included price and sales data provided by CWB.

"When modeling the behavior of the CWB, one cannot a priori assume that it acts in a perfectly competitive manner. The world barley market consists of fairly few sellers," the study said. "However, it is clear that the CWB has been able to earn additional revenue from the sale of western Canadian barley over what would have been achieved with multiple sellers."
Authors of the study included Andrew Schmitz, Richard Gray and Gary Storey, all associated with the University of Saskatchewan, and Troy Schmitz of Washington State University.

An earlier CWB-funded study by three academic economists in February 1995 concluded that single-desking of Canada's hard red spring wheat by the CWB had earned farmers an average of $13.35 per tonne extra each year over the 1980 to 1994 period.
